## Today's Agenda

- The Facebook study, and three older cases that produced today's rules
- The Belmont principles, consent, and whether this is human subjects research
- Honest reporting, prediction, and postdiction
- The assigned article, Nosek et al. (2018), and the discussion built on it
- Searching the literature in three phases, and your librarian
- CITI, and what is due before Week 4

## What Tonight Covers

- Tonight has two halves
    - First, what you owe the people whose messages you are about to analyze
    - Second, how to find out what has already been said about your topic, so you arrive at your librarian meeting with something worth their time
- You leave with three things: a non-human-subjects determination you could actually file, a preregistration stub for your own project, and a search log that becomes part of your methods section
- **Bring a topic to the second half.** You will search it live

## The Part Worth Saying Plainly

- Some of tonight is grim. The cases we teach ethics with are cases where people were hurt
- The rest of it is paperwork. Neither half is decoration
- You are not here to feel guilty about your project. You are here to be able to defend it
- You are about to analyze messages that thousands of strangers typed in public without ever being asked
- Whether that is all right depends on several things, and the first half of tonight names them

## Facebook Manipulated 700,000 News Feeds

[Kramer, Guillory, and Hancock, 2014]{.eyebrow}

- For one week in January 2012, Facebook manipulated the News Feeds of nearly **700,000 users**
- Some saw fewer positive posts from friends, and others saw fewer negative posts
- Researchers then measured what those users went on to post themselves
- Fewer positive posts produced slightly more negative content, and the reverse held
- The result was published in *PNAS* as evidence of "massive-scale emotional contagion"

## Why That Study Still Gets Argued About

- Nobody was told their emotional environment was being manipulated, and nobody could decline
- Facebook pointed at terms of service authorizing data use for "research"
- The researchers argued the manipulation was small and the effect tiny
- *PNAS* appended an **editorial expression of concern** about the consent process
- Reasonable people still disagree about whether it was ethical

Keep this one in mind. Of everything tonight, it sits closest to what you are about to do.

## Tuskegee, 1932 to 1972

- The U.S. Public Health Service studied untreated syphilis in **399 Black men** in Macon County, Alabama, for forty years
- The men were told they were being treated for "bad blood"
- Penicillin became the standard treatment in the 1940s, and the researchers withheld it
- **28 men** died of syphilis directly, **100** died of related complications, **40 wives** were infected, and **19 children** were born with congenital syphilis
- The study was federally funded, run by credentialed staff, and published for decades without objection

## Milgram, 1961

- Participants were recruited by newspaper advertisement and told it was a study of memory and learning
- Each was cast as the "teacher," while a confederate played the "learner" in the next room
- They were instructed to deliver escalating shocks for wrong answers, up to a switch at **450 volts**
- The shocks were not real. The belief that they were real, and the distress, were
- **26 of 40** participants in the baseline condition went to the maximum voltage
- Hesitation was met with scripted prods, "the experiment requires that you continue," rather than with permission to stop

## Milgram, What It Cost

- Milgram reported participants sweating, trembling, and stuttering, and in one case a seizure violent enough to stop the session
- Participants were debriefed, and the deception was total until that point
- The findings reshaped how the field understands obedience to authority, and they are still taught in every introductory course
- The argument about whether the knowledge justified the distress has never closed
- That is the point: this is not a case where the researcher was careless or malicious, and people were still harmed

## Humphreys, 1970

- Humphreys's doctoral research studied anonymous sexual encounters between men in public restrooms
- He took the role of **watchqueen**, the lookout, which let him observe without participating and without disclosing that he was a researcher
- He recorded the **license plate numbers** of the men he observed
- He traced those plates to home addresses through motor vehicle records, obtained via a contact in the police
- About a year later he changed his appearance and his car, and interviewed the men in their own homes, posing as a health-survey interviewer

## Humphreys, What It Cost

- Most of the men were married and living otherwise conventional lives
- In 1970 exposure meant criminal prosecution, loss of employment, and destroyed families
- He kept the data secure, and he argued the work reduced stigma by showing who these men actually were
- The book won a major award in sociology, and his own department fought over whether to strip his doctorate
- Both halves of that sentence are true at once, which is why the case is still assigned

## The Common Thread

- In each case people were harmed, deceived, or exposed
- In each case the researcher had institutional backing and sincere motives
- **Good intentions never were a protection.** That is the whole lesson
- Ethics is a disposition rather than a form: how you treat the people you study, and how honestly you report what you found
- What follows from that is outside accountability, which is where Belmont comes in

## Belmont: Respect for Persons

[National Commission, 1979]{.eyebrow}

- People are capable of deciding for themselves what happens to them
- **Informed consent** means understanding the study, the risks, and the right to walk away
- **Vulnerable populations** get extra protection: children, prisoners, and anyone whose capacity to consent freely is diminished
- Survey a listener about a podcast and consent is simple
- Analyze public posts and consent gets hard fast, which is your situation

## Belmont: Beneficence and Justice

- **Beneficence** carries two duties: do no harm, and maximize benefit against risk
- Harm counts as physical, psychological, social, or economic
- Content analysis usually carries minimal risk, because you work with texts and not people
- **Justice** asks whether benefits and burdens fall fairly across groups
- Tuskegee failed justice: all of the risk sat on one marginalized population while the knowledge accrued to everybody

## Consent in Practice

- Valid consent covers the study, the risks, that participation is voluntary, who to contact, and how the data will be stored
- **Deception** is sometimes defensible, and it is always paired with mandatory **debriefing**
- **Passive consent**, the terms-of-service move Facebook made, is generally not enough
- **Active consent** needs an affirmative act: a signature, a click, or a spoken yes
- **Secondary analysis** raises whether the original consent covered your use, and that question is still genuinely unsettled

## The Question That Comes First

Before anyone asks which level of review a study needs, there is a prior question: **is this
human subjects research at all?**

- Federal regulation defines a **human subject** as a living person about whom you obtain information in one of two ways
    - Through **intervention or interaction** with them
    - In the form of **identifiable private information**
- You never interact with anyone, because the messages were sent before you arrived
- The messages were **broadcast publicly**, so they are not private information
- Neither limb is met, so this is **not human subjects research**

## The Example Dataset Through Belmont

- Chat came from the **public IRC interface** and streams from the **public API**, with no IP addresses, emails, user IDs, payment data, or whispers
- Usernames are **pseudonymous** handles, usually not tied to an offline identity
- **Respect for persons** rests on public broadcast, because consent was never asked
- **Beneficence:** risk is minimal, and nothing aggregates toward identifying anyone
- **Justice:** the sample spans channels broadly, including non-gaming categories
- **You run the same walkthrough on the source you choose**, and your answers will differ

## This Determination Has Been Made Twice

- **This is not hypothetical.** Michigan State University formally determined the Twitch data **not human subjects research**, and SIUE determined the Twitter data from the NSF work the same way
- **Your project is expected to land in the same place:** a content analysis of public broadcast content is not human subjects research
- You still write and submit the determination. **The office decides, not you**, and that is true even when the answer looks obvious
- You still complete CITI, because the training is what lets you make the argument, and because the next dataset you meet may not be this clean

## Public Is Not the End of the Question

- Researchers have argued for years that "public" does not settle the ethics (Markham & Buchanan, 2012)
- In practice that obligation comes down to three rules
    - Do not aggregate in ways that could **re-identify** an individual
    - Do not republish whole chat logs verbatim
    - Do not amplify messages whose senders expected obscurity more than broadcast

## Three Cases That Would Be Human Subjects Research

Change one thing about the data and the answer flips, and then the review tiers apply:

- **Twitch whispers** are private messages, so they are identifiable private information and need expedited or full board review
- **A private Discord with the same people in it** has closed membership, which makes the same words private even though those people chat publicly elsewhere
- **An internal moderation log with platform flags on users** attaches classifications to identified people, so it most likely needs full board review

The narrowness of our corpus is what keeps it outside the definition, and that narrowness
was designed rather than lucky.

## When the Reporting Goes Wrong

- **Fabrication** is inventing data that do not exist
- **Falsification** is manipulating data or results to change the outcome
- **Selective reporting** is running many analyses and reporting only the ones that worked
- **HARKing** is forming the hypothesis after seeing the results, then writing it up as though you predicted it all along
- HARKing turns exploratory work, which is perfectly legitimate, into fake confirmatory work

## Prediction and Postdiction

[Nosek et al., 2018]{.eyebrow}

The paper draws a sharper line than "exploratory versus confirmatory":

- **Prediction** commits to the outcome before the data can inform it. The test can fail, which is the only reason passing it means anything
- **Postdiction** explains a result you have already seen. It is legitimate, often the most creative part of the work, and it is where the next prediction comes from
- The error is never doing postdiction. The error is reporting it as prediction

## What Preregistration Does

> "Preregistration of an analysis plan is committing to analytic steps without advance knowledge of the research outcomes."
>
> Nosek et al. (2018, p. 2601)

- Preregistration does not forbid exploration, and it does not ask you to know the answer in advance
- It timestamps **which of the two you were doing**, so a reader can tell a prediction that survived a real test from an explanation built after the fact

## Three Objections, and the Paper's Answers

[Nosek et al., 2018]{.eyebrow}

Nosek anticipates three objections. Read the paper for its argument, and decide whether the
answers hold:

- **"It is a straitjacket."** The answer: depart from the plan when the work demands it, and disclose the departure. A plan you deviated from in the open still tells a reader more than no plan at all
- **"It does not fit exploratory or qualitative work."** The answer: preregistration marks which claims were predicted, so work making no predictions gives up nothing by saying so
- **"It slows everything down."** The answer: it front-loads decisions you were going to make anyway, later, under worse conditions, with the results already in view

## Registered Reports, and What This Cannot Fix

- A **Registered Report** sends the plan to peer review *before* the data exist, and the acceptance stands whatever the results turn out to be
- It aims at the incentive rather than the person: whether you get published stops depending on whether the finding came out positive
- That is the same move Belmont makes: outside accountability, not private virtue
- **It would not have saved the Facebook study.** That failure happened at consent, before any analysis began
    - Preregistration disciplines what you do with data you already had the right to hold, and it says nothing about whether you had the right

## Discussion: The Preregistration Revolution {.discuss}

On Nosek et al. (2018), "The preregistration revolution," answer each in writing:

- They call it a revolution. State whether the mechanism is strong enough to change behavior on its own, or whether it rests on incentives the authors do not control
- The paper separates prediction from postdiction. Name where that line blurs most easily, and say whether you would catch yourself crossing it
- State whether preregistration is compatible with grounded theory or thematic analysis, and argue it on epistemological grounds rather than practical ones
- Name one thing a Registered Report protects that a preregistration does not

## The Second Half: The Conversation You Are Joining

- Say your piece cold in an argument that has run for years and you get dismissed as naive, or told it was settled in 2012
- A **literature review** is the disciplined act of listening before speaking, and it is how you earn the right to ask your question
- Concretely, a review does four things
    - **It situates your work** in a context you can show you understand
    - **It identifies a gap**, which is what answers "so what?"
    - **It hands you methods**: validated measures, sampling strategies, and documented limitations (Krippendorff, 2018; Neuendorf, 2017)
    - **It sharpens your question** from a vague curiosity into something you can actually do

## Phase One: Exploratory Searching

- Start broad. You are learning the terminology, the names, and which journals publish this
- **Google Scholar** comes first. It is less comprehensive than the databases, and it is fast and free
- Wikipedia is not citable, and its reference list is still a map to real scholarship
- Any good article's reference list is a map too, and repeated names mark the foundations
- Collect everything promising in **Zotero** and tag freely. Organizing comes later

## Phase Two: Systematic Searching

- The real databases are Communication & Mass Media Complete, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus
- **Boolean operators** are the syntax these databases expect: AND narrows, OR widens, NOT excludes, and `*` catches word variants

```
(livestream* OR "live streaming" OR Twitch) AND
(motivation* OR gratification* OR engagement) AND
(viewer* OR audience* OR chat)
```

- Log every search: the date, the database, the exact string, the limiters, the results, and how many you kept
- That log is a methods disclosure, not a private note

## Phase Three: Citation Chaining

- **Backward chaining:** read the references inside an article that matters
- **Forward chaining:** use "Cited by" to find who has built on it since
- The search snowballs strategically, following the network out from the work that counts most
- Ad hoc searching cannot support a later claim about the literature, because you cannot say whether what you found is representative of it
- A systematic search can be reproduced, and updated, by somebody who is not you

## Knowing When to Stop

**Saturation** is the point where more searching stops changing your understanding. You
recognize it three ways:

- Three database searches in a row turn up nothing new that is relevant
- New articles keep citing the same eight or ten sources you have already read
- You can predict what an article says from its title and abstract

Saturation does not mean you read everything. It means the map stopped changing.

## Worth Asking Your Librarian

- Which database actually indexes the journals in my area, and what does it miss?
- How do I set an alert so new work on my topic finds me instead of the other way round?
- What is the fastest route to an article the library does not hold?
- Can Zotero pull straight from this database, and how do I fix broken metadata?
- What would you search that I would never have thought to search?

## CITI, and What It Is

- **CITI** is the Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative, the research ethics training nearly every American university runs
- You complete the **Social and Behavioral Research** course and submit the completion certificate
- The modules cover the ground of this first half: the history, the principles, informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, assessing risk, and vulnerable populations
- Each module ends in a quiz you have to pass to earn the certificate
- It takes hours rather than minutes, and it saves your place, so do it across several sittings rather than one
- **CITI Ethics Certification**, 25 points, is due Monday, September 28, 11:59 PM

## Where to Register

Two pages, and the order matters:

1. **[SIUE Compliance Training](https://www.siue.edu/compliance/training/)** first. This is the route in, and it tells you how to attach your account to SIUE
2. **[CITI Program](https://www.citiprogram.org/index.cfm?pageID=668)** second, to register and work through the modules

- **Register through SIUE, not as an "independent learner."** The independent route charges you money, and the certificate does not come back to the university, so it will not count
- If you have already made an account that way, say so and we will sort it out

## Why CITI Applies to You Anyway

If your project is not human subjects research, why complete training for human subjects
research?

- Because "this is not human subjects research" is an **argument you have to be able to make**, and CITI is where the vocabulary for making it comes from
- Because the moment any project touches people directly, no IRB will look at you without it
- Because it travels: doctoral programs and research positions ask to see the certificate
- Because your non-human-subjects determination is a document you write, and writing it well is easier once you have done the training that explains what it argues against
